relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: Elijah confronts Ahab by closing the sky in words, while an entire land will bear the drought.
A word redirects the prophet away from the palace.
He hides at a wadi east of Jordan.
Water and ravens become his fragile supply line.
He follows the word into concealment.
Wild birds bring food twice each day while the stream sustains him.
The same drought he announced dries his own water.
Another word sends him beyond Israel.
A Sidonian widow is named as the person through whom survival will come.
At the city gate Elijah finds her gathering fuel and first asks for water.
He adds a request for bread while she is already walking.
She speaks the famine without ornament: one handful, a little oil, one final meal for herself and her son.
Elijah answers fear with a promise but also asks that his portion come first, creating a severe test of power and trust.
The promised abundance is not excess but enough flour and oil to endure until rain.
The widow acts, and the household—including the guest—eats through many days.
Enough remains, meal after meal, without the jar becoming a treasury.
Then the child becomes so ill that breath leaves him, and prior provision does not protect the household from grief.
The mother rejects a theology in which the prophet's presence exposes her sin by killing her son.
Elijah receives the child from her arms and carries him into his own room.
He joins her protest, accusing the Divine rather than blaming the widow.
He places his whole body into desperate prayer for the child's life to return.
The child's life returns, a singular gift rather than a reproducible technique.
Elijah gives the living son back to his mother; the reunion, not the prophet's fame, completes the act.
The widow herself names what she has learned about the truth of the word.

contemplative_note: The chapter moves from prophetic power to mutual dependence. A foreign widow feeds the prophet; the prophet later joins her protest and returns her child. Faith here cannot be separated from food security, the right to question suffering, and the refusal to blame a mother for a child's death.
